# Copper December 2009 

- After a strong finish to November official 3-month prices hit a 15-month high of $7100/t on the 3<sup>rd</sup> of December and then retreated briefly to a month low of $6833/t on the 10<sup>th</sup> .  Since then, 3-month quotes have recovered some of this lost momentum and are currently hovering around the $6900/t mark.  Market fundamentals, meanwhile, remained weak with total exchange stocks reaching their highest level since January 2004 and demand, outside of China, continued to underperform with no immediate recovery expected soon. 

- While demand prospects in China are favourable for next year one cannot ignore the large build in Chinese metal stocks this year.  According to our analysis Chinese cathode stocks will have increased by a forecast 1Mt by year end.  In terms of days of global consumption, Chinese refined copper stocks, excluding SHFE inventories, are expected to finish this year at the equivalent of 35 days. 

- The global economy is continuing to shake off the effects of its worst recession since the end of World War II.  The concerted efforts of governments and central banks around the world have successfully stabilised the financial system and prevented the recession from developing into a depression.  However, as far as copper demand is concerned the recovery has not been universal, with demand in several of the mature economies forecast to decline significantly in 2009. 

- During 2009, spot selling terms (miners to traders) have ranged from a monthly high of $71/t & 7.1c/lb back in January, to a monthly low of $12/t & 1.2c/lb in December.  This is the reverse of what occurred in 2008 when spot rates began the year at low levels, reaching LME flat in March and then rising steadily over the course of the second half of the year to $80/t & 8.0c/lb in December.  Despite the differing spot TC/RC patterns between the two years the average rates realised in each was identical at $29/t & 2.9c/lb.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Prices peak in December** After a strong finish to November official 3-month prices hit a 15-month high of $7100/t on the 3<sup>rd</sup> of December and then retre

ated briefly to a month low of $6833/t on the 10<sup>th</sup> .  Since then, 3-month quotes have recovered some of this lost momentum and are currently hovering around the $6900/t mark.  As of the 17<sup>th</sup> , the month to date average was $6974/t or 4.1% above November’s average of $6697/t and 124.5% higher than December 2008 ($3107/t).  The current high price environment continued to be supported by industrial action and ongoing wage negotiations, positive economic data from China and increased interest from the fund community.  Market fundamentals, meanwhile, remained weak with total exchange stocks reaching their highest level since January 2004 and demand, outside of China, continued to underperform with no immediate recovery expected soon. 

**Industrial action still a key factor affecting supply** In Canada, strike action at Vale Inco’s Sudbury (115kt/a Cu) and Voisey’s Bay (40kt/a Cu) nickel/copper operations continued with no resolution in sight.  As noted previously workers at the company’s Sudbury mines and metallurgical facilities downed tools on July 13<sup>th</sup> after talks broke down on bonuses, pensions and other issues.  This was followed by workers at the company’s Voisey’s Bay mine joining the strike in August.  As a consequence of the disruption we estimate that mine production at the company’s Sudbury operations could reach 50kt Cu this year, assuming that limited copper mining activities are maintained at Coleman and Garson, compared with 117kt Cu in 2008.  At Voisey’s Bay mine production is expected to total 24kt Cu, down from 55kt Cu a year earlier.  Elsewhere, production was stopped for a day at Codelco’s Chuquicamata mine in Chile on the 9<sup>th</sup> when the entrance of the mine was blockaded by unionised workers protesting over proposed new contract terms.  Meanwhile in Zambia, the Mineworkers Union of Zambia declared a dispute with Konkola Copper Mines on the 10<sup>th</sup> after a deadlock was reached in negotiations over pay.  Likewise at Mopani Copper Mines wage negotiations are still underway with union representatives seeking a 50% wage increase (see PRODUCTION). 

**Chinese construction sector is booming** Latest Chinese government statistics showed that floor space under construction had increased by 44% year on year during November and by 17.2% year to date (Jan-Nov) from the corresponding period in 2008.  Also encouraging was the news that housing starts, which are considered an important indicator of future copper demand, surged 194% in November from a year earlier.  Added to this, data on land purchases for development were up by over 20% year on year in November.  Market participants viewed this data as positive because it lent weight to the general perception that demand for copper from China’s construction sector will remain buoyant in 2010. 

**New short positions opened** Open interest in copper spiked following the 15-month peak in official 3-month prices ($7100/t) on the 3<sup>rd</sup> .

LME data pointed to the establishment of new short positions which drove prices lower, albeit moderately, between the 4th and the 10th . However, there does not appear to have been a great deal of conviction in shorting the market as it seems that participants subsequently opted to cover their shorts from the10th , with prices responding accordingly. For now, the temptation to short copper would appear to be an extremely risky strategy given the general enthusiasm for commodities, and especially copper where the general direction for this market is seen by many as a one way bet. By comparison, at the beginning of this decade commodity assets under management were just $6-10Bn. **Popularity of commodities as an asset class will continue** In its survey of institutional investors Barclays suggests that the popularity of commodities as an asset class will continue to rise with some 60% of the respondents investing in commodities to generate an absolute return with smaller numbers investing for portfolio diversification or inflation/currency hedging purposes. Interestingly, the respondents indicated a move away from passive long-only index based investments with 28% suggesting that they plan to invest in commodities via exchange traded funds and 40% using active positions managed on their behalf by third parties. If investors retain their enthusiasm for commodities and move towards more active investment strategies this could well increase the downside risk to copper prices in the short term. This is on the basis that the disconnect between market fundamentals and prices is likely to widen further leading to a bubble that will one day burst in response to unexpected economic or other unwelcome news. **Reweighting could push price lower** It will be interesting to see how the market plays out in January with the imminent reweighting of the Dow Jones-UBS and S&P GSCI commodities indexes during the early part of that month. Simplistically, the reweighting process involves a reduction in the proportion of the best performing components of the index over the past year and an increase in the proportion of the worst performing components of the index. With LME base metal prices rising by 76% on average this year the reweighting process

will result in a sell off of certain metals including copper. Whilst the market may simply shrug off this adjustment any weakness in copper prices at this time has the potential to lead the whole base metals complex lower during the reweighting process. **Exchange stocks rise for sixth consecutive month** Total exchange stocks have risen so far this month by a net 36kt to 656kt as of the 16th . This represented the sixth consecutive month of increase and overall exchange stocks, at 14 days of consumption, remained at their highest level since the beginning of 2004. Net increases were recorded on both the LME and Comex while inventories in Shanghai declined by a net 5.6kt to 95.7kt. On Comex, warrants increased by a net 8kt, to 85.7kt, while on the LME stocks rose by a net 33.6kt to 474.6kt. For the second consecutive month deliveries into LME warehouses increased on a daily basis. Once again the main recipients were warehouses in the US and South Korea where inventories rose by a net 14.1kt and 15.7kt to 270kt and 104kt respectively. This reflected a growing trend since the end of June with US and South Korean inventories having increased by a net 83kt and 103kt respectively. In the case of the US, the higher inventories were on account of falling demand, particularly from the construction sector, while in South Korea the gain reflected material redirected from both the US and Europe in order to achieve higher premia in both South Korea and in China where demand was much stronger. Year-to-date total exchange stocks have increased by a net 266.3kt as of the 16th. **European spot premia levels ease** European spot business, unsurprisingly, has remained very slow so far this month as consumers reduced their inventories ahead of year-end book squaring. As a consequence, premia for Chilean and Grade A material from Rotterdam have eased in recent weeks and are currently fetching $55/t, down $10/t from levels in November. Standard grade cathode quotes from Rotterdam also weakened, falling from $25/t in November to $20/t presently. Elsewhere, the price for Italian warrants from Livorno was unchanged at $75/t. In the term market negotiations for 2010 material are still ongoing with some market sources reporting that a number of outstanding contracts will be settled at levels lower than Codelco’s industry benchmark of $80/t. ### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 9000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - December 2009 Page 3 of 25 Copper Monthly Update **US premia little changed** US spot premia also weakened during December as consumers continued to r

un down their inventories ahead of year-end and turned their attention towards finalising contract terms for 2010 purchases. According to market sources the US situation is similar to Europe with negotiations still ongoing and with only a few deals confirmed so far. In the meantime, spot premia have fallen from 3.75c/lb in November to 3.5c/lb presently. **Chinese premia firm** In contrast to the US and Europe, Shanghai premia actually increased during the month, rising from $50/t at the end of November to $60/t presently. This has been on account of consumers purchasing metal in anticipation of robust demand at the beginning of next year. Chinese premia averaged $99/t during the year, up by 48.9% from last year’s average of $66.5/t. The significant increase helps to underline the strength of Chinese demand this year. Next year we expect that premia will remain firm as underlying demand continues to be strong. As noted earlier the outlook for the Chinese construction sector looks positive and ongoing investment within the country’s power sector remains robust. ### **Physical copper spot premia rates ($/t)** W Europe Shanghai

**Large build in Chinese stocks this year** While demand prospects in China are favourable for next year one cannot ignore the large build in Chinese metal stocks this year. According to our analysis Chinese cathode stocks will have increased by a forecast 1Mt by year end. In terms of days of global consumption, Chinese refined copper stocks, excluding SHFE inventories, are expected to finish this year at the equivalent of 35 days. And while Chinese stocks have more than doubled from their previous typical levels of 16 days, there has only been a modest uplift in stocks elsewhere (+6 days in exchange warehouses and +4 days in the world ex-China). This is a really key factor in the sense that the general feel of the market is one of little change in terms of stocks whereas, in reality, both the build up and displacement of inventories into less visible Chinese locations have been massive. It is almost impossible to know when Chinese speculators may decide to release their copper metal inventories as each will have differing financial circumstances, purchase prices and selling price objectives. We do not feel, however, that there will be a mass release in the short term because the potential returns on most other alternative investments still remain relatively unattractive and the general belief amongst Chinese speculators is that the price of copper will move higher and this could, if anything, lead to further buying opportunities. **Market surplus forecast to exceed 1Mt this year** We have raised our 2009 global market surp

lus since our last report and now forecast that supply will exceed demand by ~1.2Mt. The increase reflects revisions made to both our demand and supply forecasts. In the case of our demand estimates the lower figure reflects weakening demand in Europe, particularly in France. We now forecast that metal stocks will have risen to 75 days of consumption, their highest level since 2003. We also continue to reflect the ongoing disconnect between market fundamentals and prices and have raised our average cash LME estimate to $5170/t ($2.34/lb) this year. **Stronger prices forecast in 2010 and 2011** In 2010 we expect average prices to increase by 23.8% to $6400/t ($2.90/lb). While a little less than current quotes, this is still a very respectable level for the market relative to the fundamentals. Demand growth is forecast to rise by 6% against a background of limited supply growth (+0.5%). As a consequence the global market surplus for 2010 is expected to fall significantly to ~270kt. We do not expect supply to keep pace with extremely robust demand in 2011 which will give rise to a market deficit of ~150kt with metals stocks falling from 76 to 68 days of consumption. In tandem with these improving fundamentals we are forecasting a further increase (+3.3%) in average prices to $6613/t ($3/lb) in 2011. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - December 2009 Page 6 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Economic Developments **Pattern of winners and losers in global economic recovery reflected in construction activity** The global economic recovery, which has gained momentum through the fourth quarter on the back of significant and seemingly successful stimulus packages, has shown increasing divergence between developed and developing economies. The same can be said for the global construction market. Whilst construction output has been improving in economies such as India, China and Brazil, activity remains very subdued in the US, Europe and Japan. **Stabilisation but little sign of recovery in US residential construction** Latest housing data for the USA show further signs of stabilisation, but high unemployment and the threat of yet greater numbers of foreclosures are set to keep the recovery reasonably muted. The decline in US residential construction activity has been well documented, with the number of housing starts falling by 78% from the September 2005 high to the April 2009 low. Hopes were raised through mid 2009, when the level of housing starts began to rise. From April to July, starts increased from an annualised rate of 479,000units to 593,000 units, an increase of 24%, seemingly indicating a start to the recovery in US residential construction. However, the recovery appears to have stalled, as starts have been relatively unchanged through the second half of the year. Latest data for November showed housing starts at an annualised rate of 574,000 units, still down by 12.4% from November 2008. There are a couple of factors which could see a boost in residential construction activity in the first half of next year. The first-time h

omebuyer tax credit, originally due to expire November 30, has been extended into 2010. This should help boost demand for new homes. Secondly, thanks to the increase in new home sales triggered by low borrowing rates and the stimulus package, inventories of new homes are at 6.7 months of demand. This is down from 12.4 months of stock at the start of 2009, and almost down to levels that were the norm before the US housing crisis. The chief threat to the potential recovery in residential construction is foreclosures flooding the market. Approximately 4.2 million homes are in late-stage delinquency or have entered foreclosure, and government initiatives aimed at owners of such properties are making little progress. This problem is particularly acute in the Sun Belt states of California, Florida and Nevada, adding to the fiscal woes these states face. The large overhang of distressed properties should keep the recovery in construction activity reasonably muted through 2010. ### **US housing starts and year-on-year % change** 30 Housing starts 2500

**Japanese residential construction shows improvement, but doubts over sustainability** The Japanese housing market has shown some improvement in the past couple of months, with housing starts in October increasing by 12.3% from the August low to 67,120 units. However, they remain down by 27.1% from a year earlier. In addition, there is excess supply of residential property nationwide, and construction orders data, which is a leading indicator of housing starts, gives little indication that robust growth in housing starts is likely in the coming months. **European construction outlook equally poor** Construction data for Europe shows little sign of recovery in activity, now or in the near future. The euro zone construction PMI, charted below, shows that both residential and commercial construction activity, as well as new orders, remain below the 50 confidence level. However, it does indicate that the rate of contraction at present is slower than has been the case over the past year. This tallies with the view from the 69th Euroconstruct Conference, which took place in Zurich at the end of November. Euroconstruct reported construction output in its 19 member countries contracting by 8.4% in 2009, with negative growth in all economies bar Switzerland and Poland. Looking forward, it expects both residential and non-residential construction activity will continue to decline Metals Market Service Monthly Update - December 2009 Page 7 of 25 Copper Monthly Update in 2010, falling a further 2.2%.

_Note: Data above 50 confidence level implies an expansion whereas below the 50 confidence level implies contraction_ **China builds on construction recovery** Whilst most of the developed economies have very subdued construction activity, China is going through another boom period. The surge in bank lending in China through 2009 has spurred on a flurry of activity in the real estate sector. Floor space under construction over the first eleven months of the year is up by 17.2% from Jan-Nov 2008, but due to the downturn in early 2009, this figure fails to illustrate just how much activity has boomed recently. Breaking out the more volatile monthly figures shows that the three-month moving average of construction activity through to November is up by 54% year on year, as illustrated in the chart below. With average property prices in November increasing at the fastest pace in 16 months, the Chinese government is concerned about the development of real estate bubbles, and as a result, has scaled back some of the property stimulus measures introduced at the end of 2008 and in early 2009. Nevertheless, government sources indicate that policy remains committed to the development of affordable housing, particularly in central and western provinces. This leaves the government with a difficult balancing act; keeping speculation and prices in check without stymieing construction activity, which is essential to China’s economic growth. Although we remain optimistic about the near-term outlook for construction activity, the authorities getting the balancing act wrong is a downside risk to sustained, robust growth. ### **China floor space under construction (YoY % change – 3 month moving average)** 60

The concerted efforts of governments and central banks around the world have successfully stabilised the financial system and prevented the recession from developing into a depression. However, as far as copper demand is concerned the recovery has not been universal, with de

mand in several of the mature economies forecast to decline significantly in 2009. **Substantial downward revisions made to our demand forecasts during the year** As a consequence we have lowered our 2009 global demand estimates by a significant 0.8Mt since the end of last year. We now forecast that global refined copper consumption will decline by 5.1% this year to just above 17.1Mt. At the end of last year we were projecting a moderate fall of just 0.5% with global demand reaching ~17.9Mt. For 2010 we have lowered our estimates by just 25kt since the end of last year, despite a series of revisions made to our forecasts. The minor adjustment reflected a net 1.1Mt increase in our Chinese demand forecasts which largely offset a net 1.5Mt reduction in our Western World forecasts and a net 0.3Mt decline in our Russian demand figures. In the case of the Western World the weaker forecast reflected the knock-on effects of the adjustments made to our 2009 estimates in Western Europe, the USA and Japan. Meanwhile in Russia, the lower demand forecast reflected the expectation of lower wire rod production in 2010 following the removal of the Russian 5% export duty on cathodes earlier this year. This meant that the incentive to convert cathode into wire rod, which previously was exempt from export duties, has been removed. We now forecast that global refined copper consumption will increase by 6% next year to ~18.1Mt, before strengthening by a further 6.9% in 2011 to just under 19.4Mt. **Demand much weaker than expected in Western Europe** The region that has experienced the largest downward revision is Western Europe where we have lowered our demand estimates by a ~0.7Mt since the end of 2008. This largely reflects adjustments made to our French, Italian and German forecasts which have been reduced by ~130kt, ~195kt and ~244kt respectively. As noted previously, demand in France has been greatly reduced by the closure of the Nexan’s Chauny wire rod plant since September 17th because of strike action. Workers are objecting to the company’s decision to close the plant at the beginning of next year. It is now unlikely that the plant will re-open at all which will result in the loss of ~60kt/a next year. We now forecast that French refined copper consumption will fall by 36.2% this year, to ~240kt, and by a further 23.6% in 2010 to 185kt. **European construction sector underperforms** In Germany and France demand throughout the year has been hampered by the region’s poor performing construction and auto sectors. Construction output has only grown in Switzerland and Poland this year.  According to Euroconstruct, the greatest falls in output have been in new residential construction (22.5%) and in non-residential construction (12.7%), civil engineering is the only sector which did not contract in 2009.  In 2010 Euroconstruct is forecasting a further 2.2% decline in construction output and projects consequently, it will not be until 2012 that European construction output returns to pre-recessionary levels.  With construction being a key driver for copper consumption, whether in the form of copper wire and cable or copper and copper alloy products, demand from this sector will most probably remain weak. 

**Sharp fall in German auto production** In the auto sector German output of cars and light vehicles totalled 4.7M units in the first 11 months of the year, a year on year decline of 18.7%.  The decline would have been greater were it not for the success of the scrapping scheme which resulted in an 8.8% increase in sales to 3.8M units over the same period. However, the ending of the scheme in September is already having an impact, with car sales in November totalling 280k units, their lowest monthly level since February and raising the spectre that sales will continue to fall in the coming months.  The German automotive industry association, the VDA, suggested that new car registrations could contract by as much as 25% in 2010.  Overall Western European car production fell by 23% year on year during the first ten months of the year to 13.1M units.  As a consequence of the weak demand from the auto and construction sectors we forecast that German and Italian refined copper consumption will decline by 26% and 22% this year to ~1Mt and ~0.5Mt respectively.  For the region as a whole we expect that demand will fall by ~21.9% to ~2.7Mt, its lowest level since 1983. However, in 2010 we are f

orecasting a small recovery in European demand with consumption increasing by 2.1% to just above 2.7Mt. Supporting this growth will be ongoing demand for copper wire rod from the region’s power sector. Demand for power cable this year has benefitted from the pan-European requirements of the authorities which state that only underground cable should be used for replacement and expansion investments within the power network. This benefit is expected to continue through into 2010. **Japanese government unveils new stimulus package** Although the Japanese economy has shown signs of emerging from recession, moribund domestic demand means that there is a danger that growth could slide back, and this risk has prompted the new government to unveil a new stimulus package. The package is primarily designed to support households and small businesses, including subsidies designed to encourage the purchase of more environmentallyfriendly goods, rather than the more traditional public works spending, which has been the mainstay of government attempts to stimulate the economy since the 1990s. **Construction sector showing modest improvement** The downturn has been highly damaging to the embattled Japanese construction sector. However, the situation is improving. On a seasonally-adjusted basis, housing starts in October rose by 9% to 67Mm2 from September’s 61.2 Mm2 , which was itself 3.4% higher than in August. While the improvement is encouraging, in year on year terms starts were still down 27%. Meanwhile, the value of construction orders and the country’s 50 largest building contractors deteriorated in October, falling by 14% from September and 40% from October 2008. This weakness suggests that the strong pace of improvement in housing starts is unlikely to be maintained, with only modest growth projected into next year. **No recovery in Japan’s automotive sector** Japan’s automotive sector continues to struggle with collapse of demand for Japanese cars in the key export markets of Western Europe and the US. **India and South Korea recovered well from global recession** In Asia the economies of India and South Korea have recovered well from the turmoil caused by the global recession.  The manufacturing PMIs for each country indicate that their manufacturing sectors moved into expansionary territory at the end of the first quarter after the initial boost in activity, led by a re-stocking phase, had levelled off.  In both countries, government efforts to stimulate the economy have paid off, with South Korea getting the added fillip of a depreciation of the won which helped improve the competitiveness of the country’s exports. 

**Brighter outlook for South Korean copper demand** South Korean demand for copper has benefited from increased overseas orders for copper wire rod from China.  According to latest trade data South Korean exports of copper wire rod to China during the first 10 months of the year increased by 48% (+25.6kt) compared with the corresponding period in 2008.  Exports of copper wire rod to India also increased significantly, rising by 105% (+5.8kt) year on year during the ten-month period.  In recent years South Korean wire rod producers have concentrated on increasing their exports to India to help offset any future drop in Chinese demand as the Chinese domestic wire rod sector becomes more self sufficient.  Overall South Korean wire rod exports increased by 40% (+35.7kt), to 125kt, during the first ten months of the year from a year earlier.  Reflecting this we now forecast that South Korean refined copper consumption will increase this year, rising by 1.4% this year to 750kt.  This will represent the first annual gain since 2004, when demand increased by 4.9% to 950kt.  Demand is forecast to increase further in 2010 and 2011 by 1.9% and 2.1% to ~765kt and 780kt respectively, in line with the recovery in the global economy. 

**No improvement in US construction sector** The US construction sector also remains desperately weak.  Worse still, the outlook for the more copper-intensive non-residential construction sector is expected to remain depressed through 2010. However, while this latest reading is welcome, it would suggest that the US non-residential construction sector will remain weak for at least the first half of 2010 and probably until 2011 given the 5-12 month lead time between architectural billings and the actual start of construction. Nevertheless, one potential source of hope for non-residential construction next year is the additional government spending on infrastructure. Discussions are currently underway in Congress that could result in the release of $35Bn for ‘shovel ready’ projects in February next year. Estimates suggest that dewatering the Luanshya shaft will take between three and five years. In the meantime China Nonferrous is also continuing the development of the Muliashi SxEw project, which is expected to be commissioned next year (at the earliest). Capital costs for the 35kt/a Cu project are put at $150M.
